lines.text: A fox came to a hen house at dusk.
So the fox asked for something small: one paw by the door.
It seemed harmless. They said yes.
Next night, one feather. Then one egg.
Each time, they whispered: it's only a little.
Then the fox asked for the key.
Some even thanked it for asking nicely.
By then, saying yes was just what they did.
It's a fable. But the pattern has a name: foot in the door.
In a 1966 study, homeowners were asked to show a tiny safe-driving sign.
Two weeks later, someone else asked for a huge sign on their lawn.
Of those asked for the tiny sign first, seventy-six percent agreed.
Of those asked cold, seventeen percent.
The researchers' guess: a small yes changes how you see yourself.
So the next ask never feels like the big one.
Which yes should the hens have refused?
